lesson.title: How Old Is That Layer? Relative and Absolute Dating
lesson.summary: Geologists and paleontologists use two complementary approaches to age rocks and fossils: relative dating, which orders events without assigning a number, and absolute dating, which uses radioactive decay to assign an actual numeric age.
lesson.body:
Once a fossil is found, an obvious question follows: how old is it? Scientists answer this with two different but complementary approaches. Relative dating tells you the order in which rock layers, and the fossils within them, formed, without giving a specific number of years. Absolute dating tells you an actual numeric age, typically with some margin of error, usually expressed in years before present.

Relative dating rests on a simple, powerful idea called the principle of superposition. In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock layers, the oldest layer is at the bottom and each successive layer above it is younger, because sediment accumulates over time with newer material deposited on top of older material. By examining which layer a fossil is found in relative to other layers, and relative to fossils found in other layers, geologists can establish a relative sequence, this fossil is older than that one, even without knowing the exact age of either. Index fossils, from species that were widespread but existed for a relatively short, well defined span of geological time, let geologists correlate the relative ages of rock layers in different locations around the world, even when those layers cannot be physically traced to one another. Related principles reinforce this: the principle of original horizontality (sediment is deposited in roughly horizontal layers, so tilted or folded layers were disturbed after formation) and the principle of cross-cutting relationships (a feature that cuts across rock layers, such as a fault or an intrusion of igneous rock, must be younger than the layers it cuts through).

Absolute dating supplies the numeric ages that relative dating cannot. The most widely used method is radiometric dating, which relies on the predictable decay of radioactive isotopes. A radioactive isotope decays into a different, more stable element at a constant, measurable rate, described by its half-life, the amount of time it takes for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. Because that rate does not change with temperature, pressure, or chemical environment, measuring the ratio of remaining radioactive isotope to its stable decay product in a sample lets scientists calculate how much time has passed since the sample formed, for igneous or volcanic rock, or since an organism died, for organic material.

Carbon-14 dating is the method most people have heard of, and it is genuinely useful, but only within specific limits that are worth understanding clearly. Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about 5,730 years. Living organisms continuously take in carbon, plants from carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, animals by eating plants or other animals, keeping the ratio of carbon-14 to stable carbon-12 in their tissues roughly matched to the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, it stops taking in new carbon, and the carbon-14 already in its tissues decays away at that fixed rate while the carbon-12 stays put. By measuring how much carbon-14 remains relative to carbon-12, scientists can calculate how long ago the organism died. Because the half-life is only about 5,730 years, though, this method is only practical for once-living material, bone, shell, wood, charcoal, that is relatively recent on a geological timescale, useful out to roughly 50,000 years or so before the remaining carbon-14 becomes too little to measure reliably. Carbon-14 dating cannot date rocks directly, since rocks were never alive and never took up atmospheric carbon, and it cannot date most fossils of real geological age. Dinosaur bones, for instance, are far too old for any measurable carbon-14 to remain.

To date much older material, such as the rock layers that contain dinosaur fossils, scientists turn to other radioactive isotopes with much longer half-lives, some measured in hundreds of millions to billions of years, commonly applied to volcanic rock or ash rather than to the fossil itself. Because volcanic ash layers often form and settle just above and below the sedimentary layers containing a fossil, dating the ash layers radiometrically brackets the fossil's age between two numeric bounds, combining absolute dating of the surrounding rock with the relative position of the fossil established by superposition. In practice, relative and absolute dating are used together. Relative dating establishes the sequence of events, and absolute dating anchors that sequence to real numbers of years, and the results from independent radiometric methods applied to the same rock formations consistently agree with each other and with the ordering predicted by superposition, an important check on the reliability of both methods.
